newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU ministers set to tackle road traffic pollution.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers set to tackle road traffic pollution.

text.p: European Union environment ministers are due on Thursday to look at draft rules intended to cut air pollution from road traffic by setting tougher engine emission and fuel quality standards for cars, EU diplomats said.

Ministers are to tackle two European Commission proposals drawn up after years of consultation with the oil and car industries and launched last year amid frenzied disagreement and extensive lobbying by interest groups from all sides.
The first proposal, setting emission norms for new diesel and petrol-engined cars from the year 2000, was the target of 88 amendments adopted by the European Parliament last April.

While the European Commission rejected most of these, ministers still face several issues, including the use of tax incentives to encourage early introduction of new technologies, whether to require cold-start emissions tests and details concerning mandatory fault detection systems on vehicles.

More divisive perhaps is that Austria, Germany, Denmark and Finland want a second set of standards to kick in from 2005, for fuel and engine emissions, while others want no new figures before a Commission review.
The same four countries, backed by Luxembourg and Sweden, also want the 2000 norms tightened for pollutants such as carbon monoxide, fuel fumes, nitrous oxides and tiny soot particles.
Fuel quality rules, which prompted 53 parliamentary amendments in April, are also contentious.
The Commission rejected most of the amendments, pleasing the oil industry lobby, which had said parliament's proposals would add billions of dollars to the total bill.
Fuel quality has marked effects on engine pollution, particularly on the mandatory exhaust catalysts now fitted in EU petrol-engined cars and on the catalysts planned for diesels.
Divisions remain over benzene and sulphur content in fuel, with the Commission proposing year 2000 values for petrol of two percent benzene and 200 milligrams/kg of sulphur.
The Dutch, as EU presidency holders, propose one percent and 50 mg/kg respectively, winning the support of five countries versus the Commission's five and the variously divided others.
Delegations agree on a 2000 figure of 350 mg/kg proposed for sulphur in diesel but remain far apart on whether to set a binding figure for 2005 and on what any figure might be.
Other points at issue concern the planned phase-out of leaded petrol and the use of cleaner fuels in certain areas.
Whatever happens on Thursday, and possibly Friday if the meeting runs on, the outcome must still pass via the European Parliament, meaning a final result is unlikely before 1998.
